name: World Geography
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: Continents, oceans, countries and capitals, landforms, coordinates, time zones, map projections and climate.

lesson.intro: Geography explains where things are and why: why a capital sits where it does, why a desert forms, why one hemisphere has summer while the other has winter. Here are the big features of the planet and how maps, time zones and climate work.
objectives: Rank the continents and oceans and place them on a mental map
Name the capitals often confused with bigger cities, and say why they were chosen
Use latitude, longitude and time zones to locate places and work out local time
Explain why flat maps distort sizes, and read a map scale
Explain how latitude, altitude and oceans shape climate, biomes and population

sections.title: Continents and oceans
sections.key: There are seven continents and five oceans; Asia is the largest continent by area and by population, and the Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean.
sections.body:
Most English-language schools teach seven continents. Asia is the largest by area and by population: about six in ten of the world's people live there.

[[visual]]

Europe and Asia share one landmass, **Eurasia**, so the line between them is a convention, commonly drawn along the Ural Mountains in Russia.

Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface:

[[visual 2]]

The Pacific covers about a third of the planet, more than all the land combined. It holds the deepest known point, the **Challenger Deep** in the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 km down.

visual.title: Continents by area, million km²
visual.caption: Australia is often grouped with nearby Pacific islands as Oceania.

visual.title: The five oceans, largest first
rows: Surrounds Antarctica; many agencies now count it as the fifth ocean

sections.tip: Area and population rank differently: Antarctica is fifth by area but has no permanent residents.
sections.pitfall: Assuming area and population rank the same way. Europe is second smallest by area but third by population.

check.question: Which continent is the largest both by area and by population?
choices: Africa
Asia
North America
Europe
check.explanation: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land and holds about six in ten of its people. Africa is second on both counts.

sections.title: Capitals that trip people up
sections.key: A capital is where a country's government sits, and it is often not the biggest city: many were chosen as compromises or built on new, central sites.
sections.body:
A **capital** is the city where a country's government sits. It is often not the largest or best-known city:

[[visual]]

Many were chosen on purpose:

[[visual 2]]

Some countries split the job. Bolivia's constitutional capital is Sucre, while La Paz is the seat of government. Myanmar moved its government from Yangon to the purpose-built Naypyidaw in the mid-2000s.

visual.title: Why there?
rows: Built as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne
Partly a compromise between English- and French-speaking Canada
Built in the interior to pull development away from the coast
Replaced Lagos with a more central site
The new Turkish state moved away from Istanbul, the old Ottoman seat

sections.tip: Some countries split the job: South Africa has three capitals, Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
sections.pitfall: Assuming the biggest or most famous city is the capital. Sydney, Toronto, Istanbul, Lagos, Zurich and New York are all not capitals.

check.question: What is the capital of Canada?
choices: Toronto
Montreal
Ottawa
Vancouver
check.explanation: Ottawa was chosen in 1857, partly as a compromise between English- and French-speaking regions. Toronto is the largest city but not the capital.

sections.title: Countries: the big, the small and the landlocked
sections.key: The UN has 193 member states; Russia is the largest country, Vatican City the smallest, and about 44 countries are landlocked.
sections.body:
How many countries are there? The usual answer is 195: the 193 member states of the **United Nations** plus two observer states, the Holy See (Vatican City) and Palestine. Taiwan and Kosovo govern themselves but are recognized by only some countries, so any count is a political choice.

[[visual]]

About 44 countries are **landlocked**, with no coastline; Kazakhstan is the largest. Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884) but still keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca. Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are **doubly landlocked**: every neighbor is landlocked too.

Some borders follow natural features, such as the Pyrenees. Others are straight treaty lines, like much of the US-Canada border (the 49th parallel), or were drawn by colonial powers carving up Africa.

Russia, Turkey and Kazakhstan lie partly in Europe and partly in Asia, and Egypt reaches into Asia through the Sinai.

items.title: Largest by area
points: 1. Russia: about 17.1 million km², 11 time zones
3 and 4. United States and China, in an order that depends on how coastal waters and disputed areas are counted

items.title: Smallest
points: 1. Vatican City: under half a square kilometer, surrounded by Rome

sections.pitfall: Judging population from size on the map. Canada is the second largest country but has only about 41 million people, while far smaller Bangladesh has more than 170 million.

check.question: Which of these South American countries is landlocked?
choices: Chile
Bolivia
Peru
Colombia
check.explanation: Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s and has had no coastline since. Paraguay is South America's other landlocked country; Chile, Peru and Colombia all have long coasts.

sections.title: Rivers, mountains and deserts
sections.key: Rivers flow downhill, great mountain ranges rise where tectonic plates collide, and a desert is defined by dryness, not heat, so Antarctica is the largest.
sections.body:
Rivers flow downhill, not "down the map": the Nile flows **north**, from the East African highlands to the Mediterranean.

[[visual]]

Most great mountain ranges form where **tectonic plates** collide:

[[visual 2]]

A **desert** is defined by low precipitation, usually under about 250 mm a year, not by heat or sand. Many lie in a **rain shadow**, the dry side of a mountain range where moist air has already dropped its rain.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Great rivers
rows: About 6,650 km: usually listed as the longest
About 6,400 km (some surveys rank it longer). It carries by far the most water, about a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans

visual.title: Great mountain ranges
rows: Home to Mount Everest, 8,849 m, the highest point above sea level. Formed as the Indian Plate pushed into the Eurasian Plate; still rising a few millimeters a year
The longest continental range, about 7,000 km down western South America, where the Nazca Plate sinks beneath the South American Plate
Other major ranges, in Europe and North America

visual.title: Three deserts
rows: The largest hot desert, roughly the size of the United States
In Mongolia and China, with winters well below freezing

sections.pitfall: Thinking rivers flow south, or "down" the map. Rivers flow downhill, in whatever compass direction that happens to be.

check.question: Which of these is a cold desert, where winter temperatures stay well below freezing?
choices: Sahara
Arabian
Thar
Gobi
check.explanation: The Gobi, in Mongolia and northern China, sits in the rain shadow of the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau and has bitterly cold winters. The Sahara, Arabian and Thar are hot deserts.

sections.title: Latitude, longitude and time zones
sections.key: Latitude measures north or south of the Equator, longitude east or west of the Prime Meridian, and Earth turns 15° of longitude an hour, which sets time zones.
sections.body:
Coordinates give **latitude** first: Cairo is at about 30° N, 31° E.

[[visual]]

Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, which is **15° per hour**. So time zones are roughly 15° wide, and noon comes about an hour earlier for every 15° you travel east.

[[visual 2]]

Real zone borders follow politics too. China is wide enough for about five zones but uses one, while Russia uses eleven.

The **International Date Line** roughly follows 180°. Crossing it heading west moves the calendar forward one day; heading east moves it back one day.

items.title: Latitude
points: How far north or south of the **Equator**
0° at the Equator to 90° at each pole
Its lines (parallels) run east-west and never meet
Tropic of Cancer about 23.4° N, Tropic of Capricorn about 23.4° S, Arctic Circle about 66.5° N

items.title: Longitude
points: How far east or west of the **Prime Meridian**
Its lines (meridians) run pole to pole and meet at the poles

visual.title: Noon (solar time) at 0°. What time is it at 90° E?

steps.label: East is later, west is earlier

sections.pitfall: Swapping latitude and longitude. Coordinates give latitude first: 40° N, 74° W is New York City, while 74° N, 40° W is on the Greenland ice sheet.

check.question: Flying west from the United States to Japan, you cross the International Date Line. What happens to the calendar date?
choices: It moves forward one day
It moves back one day
It stays the same
It changes by one hour only
check.explanation: Crossing the Date Line westward skips the calendar ahead one day, which is why travelers from the US "lose" a day on the way to Asia and regain it coming back.

sections.title: Maps and projections: why Greenland looks big
sections.key: Every flat map distorts something; the Mercator projection keeps shapes and compass bearings but inflates areas toward the poles, so Greenland looks as big as Africa.
sections.body:
On many wall maps Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In reality Africa (30.4 million km²) is about 14 times larger than Greenland (2.2 million km²).

A globe is the only truly accurate map: a curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, just as an orange peel cannot be pressed flat. Every flat map, or **projection**, keeps some properties and distorts others:

[[visual]]

A map's **scale** relates map distance to real distance:

[[visual 2]]

The shortest route between two places on the globe is a **great circle**, which usually looks curved on a flat map. That is why flights from North America to East Asia arc north over Alaska.

visual.title: Three kinds of projection
rows: Angles and local shapes: a straight line is a constant compass bearing
Areas swell toward the poles: Greenland, Alaska and Antarctica look huge
Sailing. Web maps use a close variant, since it keeps street corners square
Atlases: National Geographic has used the Winkel tripel since 1998

visual.title: Reading a 1:50,000 scale

steps.label: 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm on the ground

visual.result: 4 cm on the map is 2 km on the ground

sections.pitfall: Judging sizes from a Mercator map. Places far from the Equator, such as Greenland, Canada and Russia, look much bigger than they really are.

check.question: Why does Greenland look about as large as Africa on a Mercator map?
choices: Greenland's thick ice sheet makes it larger than Africa
The Mercator projection stretches areas more and more toward the poles
Africa is drawn smaller on purpose to fit the page
Mercator maps are only accurate near the poles
check.explanation: To keep angles correct, Mercator stretches the map east-west and north-south more and more with latitude, so high-latitude places are drawn far too big. It is most accurate near the Equator, not the poles.

sections.title: Climate zones and population
sections.key: Climate depends on latitude, altitude and distance from the ocean; seasons come from Earth's tilt, and climate shapes biomes and where people live.
sections.body:
**Climate** is the long-term pattern of weather in a place. The widely used **Köppen system** has five main types: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar. Three factors shape it:

[[visual]]

**Seasons** come from Earth's tilt of about 23.4°, not its distance from the Sun. In June the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and has summer while the south has winter; in December it is reversed. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

Earth has a little over 8 billion people, about nine in ten in the Northern Hemisphere, where most land is. India and China each have more than 1.4 billion; by UN estimates India became the most populous in 2023. Since around 2007, more than half of humanity has lived in towns and cities.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: What shapes climate
rows: Near the Equator the Sun is high, so its energy is concentrated on a small area. Near the poles low-angle sunlight spreads out
Air cools about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m on average, so high mountains are cold even in the tropics
Water heats and cools slowly, so coasts have milder seasons than places deep inside a continent

visual.title: Biomes: regions with similar plants and animals
rows: Near the Equator: the Amazon and Congo basins
Dry air sinks there and blocks rain

sections.pitfall: Explaining the seasons by distance from the Sun. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter.

check.question: Mount Kilimanjaro lies close to the Equator, yet it has ice near its summit. What explains this?
choices: Its peak receives almost no direct sunlight
Cold winds blow in from the Southern Ocean
Air temperature falls as altitude increases
Ice forms anywhere that rainfall is heavy
check.explanation: Air cools by roughly 6.5 °C per 1,000 m. At almost 5,900 m, Kilimanjaro's summit is cold enough for ice despite its tropical latitude.

keyTerms.definition: Angle north or south of the Equator, from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles.
Angle east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0° to 180°.
The line of 0° longitude, running through Greenwich in London.
A line roughly along 180° longitude where the calendar date changes by one day.
A region that receives very little precipitation, usually under about 250 mm a year.
The dry side of a mountain range, where moist air has already lost its rain on the other side.
The roughly 23.4° lean of Earth's axis, which causes the seasons.
A method of flattening the curved Earth onto a map; every projection distorts area, shape, distance or direction.
A country with no coastline, such as Bolivia, Switzerland or Kazakhstan.
The shortest path between two points on a sphere; on a flat map it usually looks curved.
A large region with a similar climate, plants and animals, such as tropical rainforest, desert, taiga or tundra.

summary: Seven continents and five oceans: Asia and the Pacific are the largest.
A capital is where the government sits: Canberra, Ottawa, Ankara, Brasília, Bern.
The UN has 193 members; Russia is largest, Vatican City smallest, about 44 are landlocked.
Deserts are defined by dryness, so Antarctica is the largest; big ranges mark colliding plates.
Earth turns 15° of longitude per hour; every flat map distorts, and Mercator inflates the poles.
Climate depends on latitude, altitude and the ocean; seasons come from the tilt.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why it can be summer in Sydney while it is winter in London, and why the clocks in the two cities show different times.

questions.question: Which statement about Earth's continents and oceans is correct?
choices: Africa is the largest continent by area
The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean
The Atlantic is the largest and deepest ocean
Europe is the second largest continent by area
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface and contains the Challenger Deep, nearly 11 km down. The Atlantic is the second largest ocean, and Africa is the second largest continent after Asia.

questions.question: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra was built as the capital, partly as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne. Sydney is the largest city but not the capital.

questions.question: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.explanation: Ankara became the capital in 1923, when the new Turkish state moved its government away from Istanbul, the former Ottoman capital. Istanbul is still the largest city.

questions.question: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.explanation: Brasília was built in the interior and became the capital in 1960, replacing Rio de Janeiro. São Paulo is the largest city.

questions.question: Which country is correctly paired with its capital?
choices: Pakistan: Karachi
New Zealand: Auckland
Nigeria: Lagos
Vietnam: Hanoi
questions.explanation: Hanoi is Vietnam's capital, although Ho Chi Minh City is larger. The other options pair each country with its largest city instead of its capital; the capitals are Islamabad, Wellington and Abuja.

questions.question: What do Canberra, Brasília and Abuja have in common?
choices: Each was planned as a new capital on a central or compromise site
Each is the largest city and the main seaport of its country
Each was a colonial capital that was kept on after independence
Each is a coastal city chosen mainly for its trade links abroad
questions.explanation: All three were purpose-built capitals: Canberra as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne, Brasília to develop Brazil's interior, and Abuja for a central location in Nigeria. None is its country's largest city, and all three are inland.

questions.question: The Nile is usually listed as the world's longest river. Which record does the Amazon clearly hold?
choices: It flows through more countries than any other river
It is the only major river that flows north
It carries more water than any other river
It starts at a higher altitude than any other river
questions.explanation: The Amazon discharges roughly a fifth of all the river water that reaches the oceans, far more than any other river. The river that crosses the most countries is the Danube, and many rivers, including the Nile, flow north.

questions.question: The Nile rises in the highlands of East Africa and empties into the Mediterranean Sea. In which direction does it flow?
choices: South
North
East
West
questions.explanation: Rivers flow downhill, not "down" the map. The Nile's sources are on high ground to the south and the Mediterranean lies to the north, so the river flows north.

questions.question: Which mountain range contains Mount Everest?
questions.explanation: Everest, 8,849 m high, stands in the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and China. The range formed as the Indian Plate pushed into the Eurasian Plate.

questions.question: Antarctica is often called the world's largest desert. Why does it count as a desert?
choices: It has a thick layer of sand beneath all its ice
It has the lowest temperatures recorded on Earth
It lies hundreds of kilometers from any ocean
It receives very little precipitation each year
questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by low precipitation, usually under about 250 mm a year, and Antarctica's interior gets very little snowfall. Extreme cold alone does not make a desert; dryness does. Antarctica is in fact surrounded by ocean.

questions.question: Explain why the Andes run along the western edge of South America.
questions.answer: Along the west coast the oceanic Nazca Plate is sinking beneath the South American Plate. The collision crumples and lifts the edge of the continent and feeds volcanoes, building a long range parallel to the coast.
questions.explanation: Most great mountain ranges mark plate boundaries. Where an oceanic plate dives under a continent (subduction), the continent's edge is pushed up and volcanoes form, which is why the Andes follow the Pacific coast.

questions.question: Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. How many degrees of longitude does it turn through in one hour?
questions.explanation: 360 divided by 24 is 15. That is why time zones are roughly 15 degrees of longitude wide, and why noon comes about an hour earlier for every 15 degrees you go east.

questions.question: It is 12:00 noon, solar time, on the Prime Meridian (0°). What is the local solar time at 60° W?
questions.explanation: 60 degrees at 15 degrees per hour is 4 hours. Places to the west see the Sun later, so their time is 4 hours behind: 8:00 a.m. Adding the hours gives 4:00 p.m., which would be the time at 60° E.

questions.question: Which statement about latitude and longitude is correct?
choices: Lines of latitude run east-west and measure distance north or south of the Equator
Lines of longitude run parallel to each other and never meet anywhere
Latitude is measured east or west from the Prime Meridian at Greenwich
Longitude ranges from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the North and South Poles
questions.explanation: Latitude runs from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles along parallels that never meet. Longitude is measured from the Prime Meridian up to 180° east or west, and its meridians all meet at the poles.

questions.question: Why are the seasons reversed between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
choices: Earth's tilted axis makes each hemisphere lean toward the Sun for part of the year
Earth is much closer to the Sun during the northern summer than in winter
The Southern Hemisphere has more ocean, and the water reverses its seasons
The Sun itself gives off noticeably more heat in June than in December
questions.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees. In June the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun and gets more direct light and longer days, while the south has winter. Distance is not the cause: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter.

questions.question: Explain why places near the Equator are generally warmer than places near the poles.
questions.answer: Near the Equator the Sun is high in the sky, so its energy is concentrated on a small area. Near the poles sunlight arrives at a low angle, spreading the same energy over a larger area and passing through more atmosphere, so the ground warms less.
questions.explanation: The angle of sunlight makes latitude the main control on climate. Altitude and distance from the ocean then modify the basic pattern.

questions.question: Which statement about world population is accurate?
choices: Africa has more people than Asia
Most of the world's people still live in rural areas
China and India together hold under a tenth of humanity
About nine in ten people live in the Northern Hemisphere
questions.explanation: Most land, and the big population centers of Asia, Europe and North America, lie north of the Equator. Asia holds about six in ten people, more than half of humanity has lived in cities since around 2007, and China and India together have over a third of the world's population.

questions.question: Match each country to its capital.
questions.explanation: Each capital is less famous than a bigger city in the same country: Sydney, Toronto, Istanbul, Zurich, Casablanca and Almaty. Governments often sit in a compromise or purpose-built city.

questions.question: Put the continents in order from largest to smallest area.
questions.explanation: Asia and Africa are far ahead, the two Americas follow, then Antarctica, with Europe and Australia the smallest. Europe's population is much larger than its area rank suggests.

questions.question: Put the five oceans in order from largest to smallest.
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of the planet, the Atlantic and Indian follow, and the Southern Ocean around Antarctica is larger than the Arctic, the smallest and shallowest.

questions.question: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.explanation: Wellington, near the center of the country at the southern tip of the North Island, is the capital. Auckland is the largest city, which is the usual wrong answer.

questions.question: Which of these countries is landlocked?
choices: Chile
Turkey
Kazakhstan
Vietnam
questions.explanation: Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country; its western edge touches the Caspian Sea, which is an inland body of water with no natural link to the ocean. Chile, Turkey and Vietnam all have long sea coasts.

questions.question: It is 9:00 a.m. local solar time at 45° E. What is the local solar time at 30° W?
questions.explanation: The two places are 45 + 30 = 75° apart, and 75 / 15 = 5 hours. The western place sees the Sun later, so it is 5 hours behind: 4:00 a.m. Subtracting 45 − 30 = 15° (1 hour) forgets that they lie on opposite sides of the Prime Meridian.

questions.question: On a 1:25,000 map, two villages are 8 cm apart. How far apart are they on the ground, in kilometers?
questions.explanation: 8 cm × 25,000 = 200,000 cm. There are 100,000 cm in a kilometer, so that is 2 km. Stopping at 200,000 or converting only to meters (2,000 m) are the usual slips.

questions.question: Select every country that has territory in both Europe and Asia.
choices: Russia
Turkey
Kazakhstan
Egypt
Spain
Iran
questions.explanation: Russia spans the Urals, Turkey spans the Bosporus, and Kazakhstan has a strip west of the Ural River in Europe. Egypt spans Africa and Asia, Spain has territory in Europe and Africa, and Iran lies wholly in Asia.

questions.question: Why does a flight from Chicago to Tokyo curve north over Alaska instead of heading straight west across the Pacific as it looks on a flat map?
choices: It must refuel in Alaska
Flights are not allowed to cross the International Date Line at sea
On the curved Earth, the northern great-circle route is shorter
The winds always blow from the north on that route
questions.explanation: The shortest path on a sphere is a great circle, and between these mid-latitude cities it bends toward the pole. The flat map distorts it into a curve, which makes the straight-looking route the longer one.

questions.question: What is the latitude of the Equator, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Latitude is measured from the Equator at 0° to 90° at each pole. The Prime Meridian is the 0° line of longitude instead.

questions.question: Two cities sit at the same latitude. One is on the coast; the other is 1,500 km inland. What difference would you most expect?
choices: The coastal city has hotter summers and colder winters
Their climates are identical, because latitude decides climate
The inland city has hotter summers and colder winters
The inland city is wetter all year
questions.explanation: Water heats and cools slowly, so the ocean evens out a coastal city's seasons. Far from the sea, land heats and cools fast, giving hot summers and cold winters, a continental climate. Inland places are usually drier, not wetter.

questions.question: Why do many hot deserts, such as the Sahara and the Arabian, lie roughly 20 to 30° from the Equator?
choices: They are the places farthest from any ocean
Dry air sinks there, which blocks clouds and rain
They receive the most direct sunlight on Earth
Ocean currents carry their rain toward the poles
questions.explanation: Air that rises and rains out near the Equator descends again around 20 to 30° north and south. Sinking air warms and dries, so clouds rarely form. The most direct sunlight falls nearer the Equator, where rainforests grow.
